newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian media wage "total war" over state sell-off.
newsitem.headline: Russian media wage "total war" over state sell-off.

text.p: Russian media traded allegations of corruption against the rival tycoons who control them as a major political row over state asset sales intensified on Tuesday.

"Total information war" was business daily Kommersant's view of the mud-slinging that followed the sale of a quarter share in the state telephone holding company to a group led by a former cabinet minister and including U.S. financier George Soros.

"Vladimir Potanin and Boris Berezovsky -- No Holds Barred" ran the headline in the weekly Moscow News above a photo-montage portraying the two men as boxers. Both are key figures in banking and the media, and both supported President Boris Yeltsin's winning re-election campaign last year.

Former first deputy prime minister Potanin, 36, heads Uneximbank, Russia's third biggest, which led the Soros-backed consortium that won 25 percent of the Svyazinvest telecoms group on Friday. Government sources say Berezovsky, now on secondment to the Kremlin Security Council, backed the losing bid.

Komsomolskaya Pravda, recently acquired by Uneximbank, ran a front-page interview with First Deputy Prime Minister Boris Nemtsov, who declared that the competitive Svyazinvest auction marked a break with previous sales of state assets. Analysts say many were carved up privately among pro-Yeltsin business.

"From a sort of bandit-like amassing of capital, the country is moving to a more or less normal civilised regime," Nemtsov, 37, said. "They are going to fight us with all they have. Right up to us having to quit."
In media controlled by the losers in the Svyazinvest bidding, Nemtsov was a target for attacks.

NTV television, part of the business empire of Vladimir Gusinsky whose Most-Bank was in the losing consortium, accused unspecified bankers of using government contacts to build up funds to back a Nemtsov bid for the presidency in the year 2000.

"Everyone needs money but above all those who thirst for power need it," NTV's commentator said. "The bankers do not conceal that in effect they are creating the material-technical basis for victory in the coming presidential elections. The candidate is already known -- Boris Nemtsov."
Nemtsov, said the generally pro-reform NTV, had damaged the government more in three months than had the opposition.

Prominent ORT television presenter Sergei Dorenko opened the media attacks on the Svyazinvest sale at the weekend. He told Kommersant on Tuesday he believed Nemtsov had acted incorrectly over Svyazinvest and said he was "twitching" like a "cockroach".

ORT is 51 percent state-owned, but Berezovsky's empire also has a major stake in the channel. Dorenko said the government, in the form of privatisation chief Alfred Kokh, another of his targets, could now press the station to make management changes.
Sevodnya daily, controlled by Gusinsky, criticised Potanin, Kokh and Nemtsov and praised Dorenko's stand against them.
Nezavisimaya Gazeta, part of Berezovsky's domain, took a similar line and also ran a story suggesting Potanin himself might harbour presidential ambitions.

Berezovsky says he gave up his business interests when he joined the Security Council in December. Senior government sources told Reuters he had lobbied strongly for the losing bid in the Svyazinvest deal, along with Gusinsky.
Nezavisimaya said the government reaction to the charges by ORT's Dorenko would be a litmus test for a free press.
Moscow News lamented on the other hand that the spectacle of the media wars suggested the Russian press was no longer free.
"If at the beginning of reforms, journalists were essential to protect the public from the authorities, now the authorities need them only to defend themselves from the public," it said.
